hints: Picture each halogen in the lab at room temperature. Which one do you know as a gas, which as a fuming liquid, and which as a dark solid?
Link colour depth to position down Group 17. The colour gets darker from pale yellow green down to almost black grey.
walkthrough:
Fix the states from volatility**
Think of what you would actually see. Chlorine escapes as a gas, bromine sits as a fuming liquid that easily gives off vapour, and iodine sits as a crystalline solid. That order gas to liquid to solid already tells you boiling point rises down the group.

Fix the colours from light to dark**
Chlorine is a pale yellow green gas, bromine is a red brown liquid with brown vapour, and iodine is a grey black solid that gives purple vapour on warming. Learn them as a set in order: $\text{Cl}_2$ pale, $\text{Br}_2$ red brown, $\text{I}_2$ dark.

Final answer: chlorine: yellow / green gas
bromine: red / brown / orange liquid
iodine: grey / black solid

hints: Remember volatility means ease of turning to vapour, so less volatile means higher boiling point and stronger forces between molecules.
Compare $\text{Cl}_2$, $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ for total electrons and think how electron cloud size affects temporary dipoles.
walkthrough:
Translate volatility into forces**
Less volatile simply means harder to get into the gas phase, so boiling point increases. When a halogen boils you are not breaking the $\text{X-X}$ covalent bond, you are only separating $\text{X}_2$ molecules from each other.

Link electrons to stronger dispersion forces**
Going from $\text{Cl}_2$ (34 electrons) to $\text{Br}_2$ (70 electrons) to $\text{I}_2$ (106 electrons), the electron cloud gets larger and more easily polarised. That creates larger temporary dipoles and therefore stronger London dispersion forces. Stronger attractions need more thermal energy to overcome, so volatility falls.

Final answer: Down the group number of electrons per molecule increases.
This gives stronger London dispersion / induced dipole dipole forces between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate molecules and volatility decreases.

hints: Recall that an oxidising agent gains electrons, so compare how easily each $\text{X}_2$ molecule accepts an electron to form $\text{X}^{-}$.
Think what happens to atomic size and inner shells as you go from chlorine to iodine.
Decide whether increased nuclear charge or increased distance plus shielding wins in attracting an incoming electron.
walkthrough:
State the trend clearly**
Chlorine is the strongest oxidiser of the three and iodine is the weakest. An oxidiser works by taking electrons from another species, for example $\tfrac{1}{2}\text{X}_2 + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{X}^{-}$, so you are comparing electron gaining ability.

Picture the incoming electron**
For reduction to happen, an electron must be pulled into the outer shell of the halogen atom. In chlorine the outer shell is $n=3$, close to the nucleus with little shielding. In iodine the outer shell is $n=5$, much further out.

Balance nuclear charge against shielding**
Nuclear charge does increase down the group, but extra filled inner shells add a lot of shielding and the atomic radius increases markedly. The net attraction felt by the incoming electron therefore falls, so electron gain becomes less favourable and oxidising power decreases.

Final answer: Oxidising power decreases down the group.
Ability to accept electrons decreases down the group.
This is because increased shielding and increased distance of outer shell from nucleus outweighs increased nuclear charge, so incoming electron is less strongly attracted.

hints: Recall the simple acid base reaction that all solid halides give first, forming misty $\text{HX}$ fumes.
Think which halide ion is a strong enough reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid further to give coloured halogen vapour.
walkthrough:
Start with the common step**
Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong acid, so with $\text{NaCl}$ you get $\text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$. The $\text{HCl}$ appears as white steamy fumes. The same first step happens with $\text{NaI}$ to give $\text{HI}$.

Spot the extra oxidation with iodide**
$\text{HI}$ is a powerful reducing agent and is oxidised by hot concentrated sulfuric acid to $\text{I}_2$. That is why with $\text{NaI}$ you see characteristic purple fumes in addition to acidic fumes, while $\text{NaCl}$ shows only the white fumes.

Final answer: solid sodium chloride: steamy / misty / white fumes of $\text{HCl}$
solid sodium iodide: purple fumes of $\text{I}_2$

hints: Compare the reducing strength of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$ using the oxidising trend you stated in (b) in reverse.
Decide in each case whether sulfuric acid can oxidise the hydrogen halide that is first formed.
walkthrough:
Think in terms of who reduces whom**
Reducing power of halides increases down the group: $\text{I}^{-} > \text{Br}^{-} > \text{Cl}^{-}$. That is the reverse of halogen oxidising power. Concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ can only oxidise a sufficiently strong reducer.

Apply to chloride versus iodide**
$\text{Cl}^{-}$ is too weak a reducer, so reaction stops at $\text{HCl}$ and no $\text{Cl}_2$ forms. $\text{I}^{-}$ is a strong reducer, so it gives electrons to sulfur in $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, itself being oxidised to $\text{I}_2$ while sulfuric acid is reduced to products such as $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{S}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$.

Final answer: Concentrated sulfuric acid is not a powerful enough oxidising agent to oxidise chloride / chloride is not a powerful enough reducing agent to reduce sulfuric acid.
Iodide reduces sulfuric acid / iodide is oxidised and sulfuric acid is the oxidising agent.

hints: Identify the two key products named in the question: brown fumes and the acidic gas that decolourises acidified $\text{MnO}_4^{-}$ and causes acid rain.
Build the equation in two stages if it helps: first $\text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{HBr}$, then oxidation of $\text{HBr}$ to $\text{Br}_2$ with reduction to $\text{SO}_2$.
walkthrough:
Decode the observations**
Brown fumes must be bromine, $\text{Br}_2$. The acidic gas that decolourises acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ and contributes to acid rain is sulfur dioxide, $\text{SO}_2$. So bromide has been oxidised and sulfuric acid reduced.

Write the balanced overall change**
First $\text{HBr}$ is formed, then: $$2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Combining with the sodium salt gives the overall equation: $$2\text{NaBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Check atoms and you will see Br, S, Na, H and O all balance.

Final answer: $2\text{NaBr} + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$
Acceptable via: $\text{NaBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HBr}$ then $2\text{HBr} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Br}_2 + \text{SO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: List the normal colours: $\text{AgCl}$ is white and $\text{AgI}$ is yellow, then think which one dominates the eye in a mixture.
walkthrough:
Recall the silver halide test**
$\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{Cl}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$ white and $\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{I}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgI}(s)$ yellow. Because solution Z contains both ions, both solids form, but the strong yellow of $\text{AgI}$ masks the white $\text{AgCl}$.
Final answer: Yellow colour is due to $\text{AgI}$ precipitate (formed from $\text{Ag}^{+}$ with $\text{I}^{-}$, alongside white $\text{AgCl}$).

hints: Remember which silver halide dissolves in dilute ammonia and which does not.
walkthrough:
Separate by ammonia solubility**
White $\text{AgCl}$ dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia to give a colourless complex, while yellow $\text{AgI}$ is insoluble and remains. Dissolving away the $\text{AgCl}$ part therefore lowers the total mass of solid left in the tube.
Final answer: $\text{AgCl}$ precipitate dissolves in aqueous ammonia, leaving $\text{AgI}$ undissolved, so mass of precipitate decreases.
